author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Microscopic life on the Gulf of Maine seafloor is changing as native kelp forests retreat and invasive red turf algae spread, according to research highlighted by New Hampshire Public Radio and Maine Public.

Scientists from the University of Maine and Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences examined microbial communities associated with the region’s changing underwater habitat. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, connects the shift to a Gulf that is warming rapidly and becoming less favorable for some native kelp.

Kelp is a foundational species: its underwater forests provide structure, food and shelter for a wide range of marine life. When low-growing turf algae replace it, the visible habitat changes and so do the bacteria and other microbes living around it. Those organisms help cycle nutrients and can influence whether an ecosystem resists disruption or recovers afterward.

Researchers said the long-term consequences are not yet clear, making continued monitoring important. The findings matter along New Hampshire’s short coastline because the Gulf functions as one connected system. Changes first detected on the ocean floor can ultimately affect fisheries, water quality and coastal communities that depend on a healthy marine food web.
dek: Researchers found that warming waters and the spread of invasive turf algae are changing microscopic communities on the seafloor, with uncertain effects on ecosystem recovery.
headline: Gulf of Maine study tracks microbial shifts as kelp forests retreat
